title: Runlet Forge: unified repair command library and task scheduler
creator: Ava Chen
description:
Background:
Redwood on-call and support engineers maintain a large corpus of one-off scripts and fragmentary repair steps (shell scripts, admin API calls, Playbook snippets). These are brittle, hard to test in dry-run, and frequently duplicated across teams. Runlet Forge is a small developer-facing framework that turns these fragments into composable, idempotent 'runlets' with first-class scheduling, dry-run, and telemetry.

Goals:
1) Provide a typed, small-surface API for writing runlets that encapsulate: preconditions, optimistic checks, execution, compensating action, and post-checks.
2) Integrate with Console runbooks: make runlets discoverable, linkable from incidents, and runnable by non-engineers with guardrails.
3) Offer a lightweight scheduler and sequence runner to compose runlets into larger recovery flows with checkpointing and resume on failure.
4) Ensure every runlet emits standardized telemetry (start/finish, duration, success/failure, idempotency markers) and can be dry-runned safely against a simulated environment.

Design summary (current iteration):
- Runlet DSL: a small Python/TS library with annotations for inputs, outputs, and safety level. Each runlet exposes run(), dry_run(), and rollback() methods.
- Execution harness: a sandboxed runner that executes runlets in a containerized environment with KMS access and audit logging.
- Scheduler: cron-like scheduling with concurrency controls and automatic backoff. Runs persist intermediate checkpoints to the runlet-store (append-only ledger).
- Console integration: UI to list runlets, show last runs, allow authorized users to trigger runlets (with approval flows for high-safety actions).
- Safety fence: policy layer that checks customer_impact labels and requires multi-approver rollouts for runlets that touch production clusters.

Trade-offs and open decisions:
- Language: prototyping in Python speeds iteration for SREs, but long-term we may add a TypeScript SDK for Node-based automations. (Open: schedule for TS SDK).
- Persistence: using an append-only store simplifies forensics but increases storage usage; we will implement retention policies per project.
- Execution surface: sandboxing improves safety but adds cold-start latency. To mitigate, we plan a warm-pool of lightweight runners for common runlets.

Acceptance criteria:
- Three production runlets migrated from ad-hoc scripts (db-compact, scale-down-stale-workers, reindex-embeddings) and executed successfully in dry-run and one live run.
- Runlet telemetry visible in Console (per-run traces, latencies, and SLO breaches).
- UI for scheduling a runlet with optional approval step and audit trail.
- Automated tests and a local simulator for dry-run validation.

Rollback / Safety plan:
- All runlets require a rollback implementation unless explicitly marked read-only.
- For high-impact runlets, enable pre-approved rollback policies and automated halting on unexpected invariants.
- During rollout, restrict execution to a 'canary' project and enable broad telemetry alerts.

Metrics to track:
- # of runlets authored and # of runs per week
- Success rate and mean time to recover when runlets are used in incidents
- Dry-run to live-run drift rate (differences in outputs)
- Number of approvals requested and time-to-approval for gated runlets
